h1: Recipe Scaling Calculator — Instantly Scale Any Recipe Up or Down
description: Scale any recipe to any serving size in seconds. Enter your original servings, target servings, and up to 5 ingredients. Smart unit conversion and baking-specific leavening adjustments included.

intro: Want to double a dinner recipe for guests, or cut a batch of cookies in half? This calculator gives you the exact scaled amount for each ingredient in one step. Enter your original serving count, target serving count, and up to 5 ingredients with amounts and units. **Smart unit conversion** automatically switches cups to tablespoons when results fall below ¼ cup, ounces to pounds when they exceed 16 oz, and grams to kilograms at 1000 g. Eggs are rounded to the nearest whole unit. Leavening agents (baking powder, baking soda) are automatically capped at ~78% of linear scaling for scale-ups above 1.5× — this prevents bitter taste and collapse that comes from too much chemical leavening.
keyTakeaway: Scale factor = Desired Servings ÷ Original Servings. Apply that multiplier to every ingredient. Exception: leavening agents scale at only 75–80% of linear when you double or triple a recipe. A 4→12 serving recipe (3× scale) turns 1 cup flour into 3 cups, but 1 tsp baking powder into ~2.3 tsp — not 3 tsp.

explanation:
## How to Scale a Recipe: The Formula

Recipe scaling uses one number — the **scale factor** — applied to every ingredient:

```
Scale Factor = Desired Servings ÷ Original Servings
Scaled Amount = Original Amount × Scale Factor
```

Examples:
- 4 → 8 servings: scale factor = **2×**
- 4 → 12 servings: scale factor = **3×**
- 4 → 2 servings (halving): scale factor = **0.5×**

## Common Scale Factors — Quick Reference Table

| Original | Target | Scale Factor |
|---|---|---|
| 2 servings | 4 | 2× |
| 4 servings | 8 | 2× |
| 4 servings | 12 | 3× |
| 6 servings | 2 | 0.33× |
| 8 servings | 20 | 2.5× |
| 10 servings | 50 | 5× |
| 50 servings | 200 | 4× |

## Smart Unit Conversion Rules

Raw scaled values are automatically converted to the most practical unit:

| Condition | Conversion Applied |
|---|---|
| Scaled cups < 0.25 | Convert to tablespoons (1 cup = 16 tbsp) |
| Scaled tablespoons < 1 | Convert to teaspoons (1 tbsp = 3 tsp) |
| Scaled oz ≥ 16 | Convert to pounds (16 oz = 1 lb) |
| Scaled g ≥ 1000 | Convert to kilograms |
| Scaled ml ≥ 1000 | Convert to liters |

## Worked Example: Chocolate Chip Cookies from 4 to 12 servings (3×)

| Ingredient | Original | Scale Factor | Scaled |
|---|---|---|---|
| All-purpose flour | 1½ cups | 3× | **4½ cups** |
| Butter | 8 oz | 3× | **24 oz → 1.5 lb** |
| Granulated sugar | 6 tbsp | 3× | **18 tbsp → 1 cup + 2 tbsp** |
| Baking soda | 1 tsp | 3× (capped ~78%) | **~2.4 tsp** |
| Eggs | 2 whole | 3× | **6 eggs** |

## Leavening Exception: Why Baking Powder Does Not Scale Linearly

Baking powder and baking soda work via a chemical reaction that has a ceiling. Using too much produces:
- Bitter or metallic taste
- Over-risen structure that collapses in the oven
- Dense or gummy crumb

**Rule of thumb (per King Arthur Baking):** for scale-ups above 1.5×, increase leavening to only 75–80% of the linear amount. This calculator applies that cap automatically when you label an ingredient as leavening.

## Limitations

**Eggs:** Fractional eggs must be rounded. For precision work, beat a whole egg (≈3 tbsp / 50 g) and measure by volume.

**Salt and spices:** Flavor perception is not strictly linear. Scale to 75% first, then taste and adjust.

**Pan size:** Doubling batter volume does not double bake time — surface-area-to-volume ratio changes. Check doneness by internal temperature.

**Cooking time:** This calculator does NOT adjust cooking times. Larger batches may need 10–25% more time; smaller batches may need less.

faq.q: How do I double a recipe — what is the formula?
faq.a: Divide desired servings by original servings to get the scale factor (2 for doubling), then multiply every ingredient by that number. Example: a 4-serving recipe doubled to 8 gives scale factor 2. One cup of flour becomes 2 cups, 2 eggs becomes 4 eggs, and 1 tsp baking powder becomes ~1.5 tsp (capped at 78% of 2 tsp).

faq.q: How do I halve a recipe?
faq.a: The scale factor is 0.5. Multiply every ingredient by 0.5. Two cups of flour become 1 cup. One egg becomes 0.5 — round to 1 egg (or beat one egg and use half, about 1.5 tbsp). The calculator handles unit conversion automatically: ½ cup becomes 8 tablespoons for easier measurement.

faq.q: Why should baking powder not be scaled linearly when tripling a recipe?
faq.a: Chemical leavening has a saturation effect. Tripling baking powder linearly produces excess CO₂ that creates a bitter taste and an over-risen structure that collapses. Professional bakers use 75–80% of the linear amount when scaling up more than 1.5×. For a 3× scale-up, that means using ~2.3 tsp instead of 3 tsp per original 1 tsp.

faq.q: Does scaling a recipe change the cooking time or temperature?
faq.a: Temperature stays the same. Time may increase by 10–25% for larger batches in the same vessel (more mass takes longer to heat through), or decrease slightly for smaller batches. Never rely on a fixed timer — check doneness with an instant-read thermometer or the toothpick test.

faq.q: How do I scale a recipe that uses 3 eggs to get a fractional egg?
faq.a: The calculator rounds eggs to the nearest whole unit. For precise fractions, beat one large egg (about 3 tablespoons / 50 g) and measure the exact proportion by volume. For example, ⅔ of an egg is about 2 tablespoons. Recipes like custards or soufflés may need this precision; most everyday recipes tolerate rounding.

faq.q: What is the scale factor to go from 6 servings to 20 servings?
faq.a: Scale factor = 20 ÷ 6 = 3.33×. Every ingredient is multiplied by 3.33. One cup of flour becomes 3.33 cups (3 cups + 5 tbsp). The calculator converts units automatically so you never need to do that math manually.

faq.q: Why does the calculator convert ⅛ cup to tablespoons?
faq.a: Measuring ⅛ cup with a standard measuring set is awkward and imprecise. 2 tablespoons is the identical volume and far easier to measure accurately. The conversion threshold is 0.25 cups (4 tablespoons). Below that, the result is displayed in tablespoons — or teaspoons if below 1 tablespoon.

faq.q: Can I use this to scale a cocktail batch from 1 drink to a pitcher?
faq.a: Yes — cocktail scaling is purely linear (no leavening concerns). If a single margarita uses 1.5 oz tequila, 1 oz lime juice, and 0.5 oz triple sec, scaling to 12 drinks gives 18 oz tequila, 12 oz lime juice, and 6 oz triple sec. Use ml or oz as units. Note that ice dilution increases non-linearly in large punches.

faq.q: What units does the calculator support?
faq.a: US volume (cups, tablespoons, teaspoons), US weight (oz, lb), metric weight (g, kg), metric volume (ml, L), and whole-unit counts (eggs, pieces). Mixed US/metric across ingredients in the same recipe is fully supported.

faq.q: Is this calculator suitable for commercial or restaurant-scale recipes?
faq.a: The arithmetic is correct for any multiplier. For commercial kitchens, also account for: equipment capacity per batch, cooking losses from evaporation and trim waste, and purchasing pack sizes. The leavening cap is especially important at high multipliers (5× and above). Always test-batch before a full production run.

example.title: Example: Tripling a cookie recipe from 4 to 12 servings
steps: **Scale factor**: 12 ÷ 4 = 3×, the multiplier for every ingredient.
**Baking soda (leavening)**: 1 tsp would be 3 tsp linearly, but it is capped at ~78% to avoid a bitter taste → 2.56 tsp.
